phonemes.desc: Voiced alveolar stop [d], as in English 'door'; Welsh initial d is fully voiced.
Long close-mid back rounded [oː] — the long Welsh ô that modern orthography marks with the circumflex; a pure, sustained 'oh', never the diphthong of English 'doe'.
Alveolar nasal [n], closing the single syllable cleanly, as in English 'dawn'.

pronunciation.approximation: 'DOHN' — one syllable, one long pure 'oh' held steady, like English 'dawn' with the vowel kept clean and simple.

kin.label: Middle Welsh
kin.form: Don — the manuscript form in the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest, written without any length mark.

kin.label: Modern Welsh
kin.form: Dôn — the same name with the circumflex that modern orthography uses to mark the long vowel.

kin.label: Welsh river-name
kin.form: Dyfrdwy, the Welsh name of the River Dee, from Common Celtic *Dēwā, 'the goddess' — the name's closest living relative in the landscape.

kin.label: Irish comparison
kin.form: Danu (or Dana), the shadowy mother of the Túatha Dé Danann — the standing comparison in the handbooks, never an equation.

pronunciation.note: Don is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the temple follows the Middle Welsh manuscript spelling Don — three plain ASCII letters, with no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Modern Welsh scholarship writes Dôn with a circumflex, but that mark is a modern length-sign, not a letter the manuscripts carry; the normalized temple form preserves it only in the pronunciation record, not the spelling. The etymology is honestly uncertain: derivation from Common Celtic *dēwā 'goddess' — the root the Welsh still hear in Dyfrdwy, the Dee — is the traditional reading, while a river-name origin is also argued; the handbooks mark the question open.

domains.title: Mother of Gods
domains.subtitle: Plant Dôn — the children named for the mother
domains.lead: Dôn is the matriarch of the Mabinogi's magical house: sister of Math fab Mathonwy, lord of Gwynedd, and mother of the great kindred the Welsh tradition called Plant Dôn, the Children of Dôn — Gwydion the enchanter, Gilfaethwy his brother, Arianrhod of the star-castle, Gofannon the smith, and Amaethon the ploughman. She is the only major figure of the Four Branches who never speaks, acts, or appears: the whole of the Fourth Branch happens among her children and her brother, and she is present only in the names they carry — uab Dôn, son of Dôn; uerch Dôn, daughter of Dôn.

cards.name: Gwydion and Gilfaethwy
cards.desc: The sister-sons at Math's court: Gwydion the enchanter, 'the best teller of tales in the world', and Gilfaethwy his brother — named, always, as sons of Dôn.

cards.name: Arianrhod ferch Dôn
cards.desc: The daughter proposed for Math's footholder, tested by the wand, mother of Dylan and Lleu — and the proudest, most wounded figure of the Fourth Branch.

cards.name: Gofannon and Amaethon
cards.desc: The craftsman-sons of Culhwch ac Olwen: Gofannon the smith and Amaethon the ploughman, without whom the giant's impossible tasks cannot be done.

cards.name: Plant Dôn
cards.desc: The Children of Dôn — the Welsh divine kindred named for its mother, the standing parallel to Ireland's Túatha Dé Danann.

symbols.name: The matronymic (uab Dôn)
symbols.meaning: 'Son of Dôn' — the mother-name standing at the head of every child's name, her whole presence in the text

symbols.name: Math's wand
symbols.meaning: Her brother's instrument of testing and transformation, laid across her children's fates — the power of the uncle's house over the mother's

symbols.name: Plough and anvil
symbols.meaning: Amaethon's plough and Gofannon's smithy — the crafts of cultivation and making that her sons carry into the oldest tale

symbols.name: The Dee (Dyfrdwy)
symbols.meaning: The river the Welsh still call 'the goddess' — *Dēwā, the name's closest living relative, flowing through the real landscape

symbols.name: The star-castles
symbols.meaning: Caer Arianrhod and Caer Gwydion — her daughter's and her son's halls written into the Welsh night sky by later tradition

mythology.lead: Dôn has no myth of her own — no tale, no speech, no deed the sources record. What she has is a family, and the family is the mythology: the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi unfolds among her children and her brother Math, and the oldest Arthurian tale cannot finish its tasks without two more of her sons. Every witness names her the same way — as the mother in the matronymic — and the Welsh tradition built its northern divine house around exactly that: Plant Dôn, the Children of Dôn.

myths.title: The Sister-Sons at Math's Court
myths.text:
The Fourth Branch opens at the court of Math fab Mathonwy, lord of Gwynedd — who cannot live unless his feet rest in a virgin's lap, except when war is in the land — and it introduces the great men of that court by their mother's name: Gwydion and Gilfaethwy, sons of Dôn, Math's own sister-sons, his nephews and his company. Gwydion is 'the best teller of tales in the world'. It is these two who set the branch's whole tragedy in motion: Gilfaethwy desires Goewin, the maiden of the foothold, and Gwydion engineers the remedy — a war against Pryderi of Dyfed, bought with conjured stallions, hounds, and shields that vanish after a day, so that the king marches south and the rape can happen.

Through all of it — the war, the crime, the three years of animal-shape punishment — the mother never appears. Dôn is present in the text exactly as a name inside other names: uab Dôn, son of Dôn, the matronymic the tale attaches to her children every time it introduces them. The most consequential family in Welsh prose walks the stage under her name, and she never once walks it herself.

myths.title: Arianrhod ferch Dôn and the Wand
myths.text:
When Math needs a new footholder after Goewin, Gwydion proposes his own sister: 'Seek for you a maiden... here is Arianrhod daughter of Dôn.' The maiden is summoned and asked if she is a virgin; she answers that she does not know but believes she is. Math makes her step over his magic wand, and as she steps she drops a fine yellow-haired boy — Dylan, who at once makes for the sea and takes the sea's nature, Dylan Eil Ton, son of the wave — and, all but unnoticed, 'something small' that only Gwydion marks, wraps in a cloth, and hides in a chest at the foot of his bed. From the chest comes the boy who will be Lleu.

Arianrhod, shamed before the whole court, refuses the boy and lays upon him the three tynghedau — the fated destinies — that he shall have no name until she names him, no arms until she arms him, and no wife of any race then on earth. The rest of the branch is Gwydion undoing his sister's curses by craft. Dôn's daughter is the Fourth Branch's proudest and most wounded figure — and Dôn is present, once again, only in the patronymic: uerch Dôn, daughter of Dôn.

myths.title: The Ploughman and the Smith
myths.text:
The oldest of the Arthurian tales sends Culhwch to win Olwen, daughter of the chief giant Ysbaddaden Bencawr, who answers the suit by naming the anoethau — the long roll of impossible tasks the suitor must perform before any wedding. Two of Dôn's sons stand inside that list, because the tasks cannot be done without them. Amaethon fab Dôn must be fetched to till the giant's ground: no ploughman alive can work that land but him. And Gofannon fab Dôn, the smith of the divine house, must be brought to the work of the headlands — the craft that prepares the ground is his.

The passage is the Welsh tradition's clearest statement of what the Children of Dôn are: not a royal house in the ordinary sense but a house of powers — enchantment, the plough, the forge — each child a function the world cannot do without. Agriculture and smithcraft, the two oldest arts of civilization, belong to the matriarch's sons.

myths.title: The Futile Battle
myths.text:
The Welsh triads keep a battle for the house of Dôn. Among the Three Futile Battles of the Island of Britain stands Cad Goddeu, the Battle of the Trees, fought — the triad says — on account of a bitch, a roebuck, and a lapwing that Amathaon fab Dôn brought away from Annwn, the Otherworld. A theft of three creatures, and a war.

The Book of Taliesin's poem Kat Godeu remembers the same war from the other side of the family: it is Gwydion who enchants the trees of the forest into an army — alder at the front, oak in the thick of it — against Arawn of Annwn. One son's theft begins the quarrel, another son's enchantment fights it; and behind both, again, the mother who gives the house its name and never raises a hand in it.

myths.title: Plant Dôn
myths.text:
Welsh tradition organized its divine and heroic world by the mother's name. Plant Dôn, the Children of Dôn, stands beside Plant Llŷr as one of the two great kindreds of the Mabinogi world, and the genealogical tracts give the matriarch a lineage: Dôn daughter of Mathonwy — which makes her sister to Math fab Mathonwy and explains why her children move so freely in his court. The name-list of her children runs across the sources: Gwydion, Gilfaethwy, and Arianrhod in the Fourth Branch; Gofannon and Amaethon in Culhwch ac Olwen.

Later genealogies lengthen the list and supply what the tales omit — a husband, Beli Mawr — but the Mabinogi itself gives Dôn neither husband nor a single word of speech. She is the only major figure of the Four Branches who never appears, and the only one whose name all the others carry. The house is hers because the names are hers; nothing more was ever written, and nothing more was needed.

lore.syncretism: Dôn's great comparison is Irish, and it is as old as modern Celtic studies: [[danu|Danu]] (or Dana), the equally shadowy mother after whom the Túatha Dé Danann — the peoples of the goddess Danu — are named. A Welsh divine kindred called the Children of Dôn and an Irish one called the peoples of Danu look like two faces of one inheritance, and MacKillop and Koch both register the comparison as standard. But it is a comparison, not an equation: no Welsh text identifies the two names, and the philology is genuinely disputed. The traditional reading derives Dôn from Common Celtic *dēwā, 'goddess' — the very word the Welsh language keeps in Dyfrdwy, its name for the River Dee — while a river-name origin, matching the continental Dānuvius (Danube) and the English Don, is also argued; the handbooks leave the question open rather than resolve it. Inside the Welsh corpus her closest kin are the tradition's other mothers and queens: [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]], the Great Queen of Dyfed, and, in later genealogical speculation, her pairing with [[beli|Beli Mawr]] as father of her children — a marriage the genealogies assert and the Mabinogi never mentions. Her husbandless, speechless sovereignty has no exact parallel anywhere in Celtic literature: she is the matriarch reduced to pure name.
lore.culturalLegacy: Dôn rode into English on the same wagon as the rest of the Mabinogi: Lady Charlotte Guest's translation (1838–49) first carried the Fourth Branch into print, and the antiquarian mythography that followed made Plant Dôn the standard label for the northern divine kindred — the house of Gwydion, set beside the house of Llŷr, in every Victorian account of the Welsh gods. Twentieth-century scholarship fixed her place with precision: Ifor Williams's Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi (1930) established the text, Mac Cana's The Mabinogi read the Fourth Branch as the masterpiece of Welsh prose, and the great encyclopedias — Koch's Celtic Culture and MacKillop's Dictionary — gave the matriarch her standing head-words, Danu comparison and all. Her widest modern audience came through a children's classic: Lloyd Alexander's Chronicles of Prydain (1964–68) made 'the Sons of Don' the ruling house of Prydain, with Math son of Mathonwy and Prince Gwydion at Caer Dathyl — her name on the throne of the best-loved Welsh-derived fantasy ever written. Modern Druid and pagan practice honours her as the Welsh mother-goddess and mother of the magical line, and the Welsh sky keeps her children's names: Caer Gwydion, the Milky Way, and Caer Arianrhod among the stars.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Dôn is the matriarch who never speaks. Every other great figure of the Four Branches is given a scene, a speech, a deed — Gwydion his enchantments, Arianrhod her curses, Math his wand — and Dôn is given nothing but the space before her children's names. Yet the whole architecture of the tale leans on that silence: the northern house of Welsh mythology is not the house of Mathonwy her father, or of Math her brother, but the Children of Dôn, the kindred named for the mother. The sources are telling us something about where authority lived in the world behind the tales — that the line itself could be reckoned through the woman, and the name that organized a pantheon could be hers alone.

Her restoration is like her: three plain letters, hidden in plain sight. Don is an English word, an English river, a Spanish title — and underneath all of them the Welsh mother of gods, carrying a name the tradition glossed as 'goddess' itself. The project rescues diacritics from the address bar; it cannot rescue a scene the manuscripts never wrote. What it can do, and does here, is keep the mother-name at the head of the house, spelled exactly as the White Book and the Red Book spell it, and say plainly what the record is: a goddess made of her children's names, and a name made of nothing but itself.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in Middle Welsh in the Latin alphabet as Don — attested in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1375–1420), the two great manuscripts of the Mabinogi. Modern Welsh orthography writes Dôn with a circumflex, but that mark is a modern length-sign for the long vowel, not a letter any manuscript carries; the project therefore follows the manuscript form, and the name stands in Tier 2 by the mechanical rule — no diacritic, no distinctive letter, nothing for ASCII to lose. Because the name is pure ASCII — and also an ordinary English word and river-name — its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: don.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none. The temple is served at /sites/don/ in the meantime.

lore.archaeology: Dôn is a textual figure: no temple, votive deposit, or inscription names her, and the epigraphic record of early Wales — the Latin and ogham memorial stones catalogued by Nash-Williams — records personal names in funerary formulae, not theonyms. Her evidence is manuscript evidence. The Fourth Branch survives complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth MSS 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1375–1420), with earlier fragments in Peniarth 6; Culhwch ac Olwen is preserved in the same two codices; the Book of Taliesin (NLW Peniarth MS 2, early fourteenth century) holds Kat Godeu. The tales' date of composition is debated, most often placed in the later eleventh or twelfth century. The geography of her house is real — Gwynedd and Arfon in the north-west of Wales, where Math's court and Arianrhod's castle stand in the tale — but no sanctuary of hers is known. The closest thing to a material trace of the name is a river: Dyfrdwy, the Welsh name of the Dee, continues Common Celtic *Dēwā, 'the goddess', and keeps the matriarch's name-element flowing through the landscape to this day.
